title: The OGLE Collection of Variable Stars. Over 1.3 Million Human-Verified Eclipsing and Ellipsoidal Binaries in the Milky Way
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, submitted to Acta Astronomica
summary: We present a new release of the OGLE collection of eclipsing and ellipsoidal binary systems in the Galactic bulge and disk. The catalog contains 1 330 024 objects, including 1 280 765 eclipsing binaries and 49 259 ellipsoidal variables, nearly three times as many systems as the previous editions of the OGLE collection. The selection and classification process involved expert visual inspection of the light curves. The catalog incorporates all available OGLE-II, OGLE-III, and OGLE-IV photometry, extending the observational baseline to nearly 28 years for some objects. The orbital periods and other observational parameters of previously known systems have been updated. We present basic statistics of the sample and highlight selected rare and unusual systems.

AI.tldr: A new OGLE catalog of eclipsing and ellipsoidal binary systems toward the Galactic bulge and disk, containing 1,330,024 objects (1,280,765 eclipsing binaries and 49,259 ellipsoidal variables), roughly three times larger than previous editions.
AI.motivation: Prior OGLE editions of the eclipsing/ellipsoidal binary collection were substantially smaller; the release aims to provide a much larger, expert-validated, homogeneous sample with long observational baselines for studies of binary populations in the bulge and disk.
AI.method: Identification and classification of candidates via expert visual inspection of light curves, combining all available OGLE-II, OGLE-III, and OGLE-IV photometry (baseline up to nearly 28 years); previously known systems had their orbital periods and other observational parameters updated.
AI.result: A catalog of 1,330,024 objects (1,280,765 eclipsing binaries, 49,259 ellipsoidal variables), about three times the previous editions, with updated parameters; basic sample statistics are presented and selected rare and unusual systems are highlighted.
AI.conclusion: The enlarged, visually vetted OGLE binary catalog with multi-decade photometry offers an expanded resource for statistical studies of eclipsing and ellipsoidal binaries and for identifying peculiar systems.

title: Rediscussion of eclipsing binaries. Paper 33. The A-type system CW Canis Majoris in the PLATO southern field
comment: Accepted for publication in The Observatory. 14 pages, 5 tables, 5 colour figures
summary: CW CMa is a detached eclipsing binary containing two A0 V stars in a circular orbit of period 2.12 d. We analyse the light-curves of this system from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) together with published radial velocity measurements to determine the masses and radii of the component stars to high precision, obtaining masses of 2.087 +/- 0.022 Msun and 1.972 +/- 0.024 Msun, and radii of 1.841 +/- 0.012 Rsun and 1.748 +/- 0.014 Rsun. We detect a changing orbital period over the four available TESS sectors indicative of the presence of a companion on a wider orbit. We develop a new method to determine the effective temperatures of the component stars using their measured radii, the Gaia parallax, and surface-brightness calibrations to reduce the degeneracy between temperature and extinction. The method gives temperatures of 9850 +/- 280 K and 9570 +/- 270 K and an interstellar extinction of A(V) = 0.32 +/- 0.06 mag. The properties of the system can be matched by theoretical models for a subsolar metal abundance (Z = 0.010) and an age of 400 +/- 20 Myr. CW CMa has been selected as a target for the PLATO satellite, with which it will be observed for at least two years.

AI.tldr: CW CMa is a detached double-lined eclipsing binary of two A0 V stars (P = 2.12 d) whose fundamental stellar parameters are precisely measured from TESS light curves plus published radial velocities, revealing a hidden wider-orbit companion, with temperatures and extinction derived by a new radius+parallax+surface-brightness method.
AI.motivation: Detached eclipsing binaries are primary benchmarks for testing stellar evolution models, but accurate parameters require proper handling of the temperature–extinction degeneracy. CW CMa, a bright A-type system already selected as a PLATO target, offers an opportunity to obtain high-precision masses, radii and temperatures for calibrating models.
AI.method: Joint analysis of four TESS sectors of light curves with published radial velocities to solve for masses and radii; eclipse-timing analysis to search for orbital period changes; a new technique to determine effective temperatures from measured radii, the Gaia parallax and surface-brightness calibrations, thereby breaking the temperature–extinction degeneracy; comparison with theoretical isochrones.
AI.result: Masses of 2.087 ± 0.022 Msun and 1.972 ± 0.024 Msun; radii of 1.841 ± 0.012 Rsun and 1.748 ± 0.014 Rsun. A changing orbital period across the four TESS sectors indicates a third body on a wider orbit. Temperatures of 9850 ± 280 K and 9570 ± 270 K, with A(V) = 0.32 ± 0.06 mag. The system is matched by models with subsolar metallicity (Z = 0.010) at an age of 400 ± 20 Myr.
AI.conclusion: CW CMa is a well-characterized benchmark A-type binary with ~1% masses, ~0.7% radii and ~3% temperatures, plus evidence of a hierarchical companion and a subsolar-metallicity, ~400 Myr evolutionary state; its two-year PLATO observation will further refine these parameters and support asteroseismic and model calibration work.

title: Sherlock 'Chrones: The Curious Case of NGC 6791 and Asteroseismic Targets Therein Reveals Mixing Length Dependence on Evolutionary Stage
comment: 29 pages, 16 figures. Submitted to ApJ. This version follows implementation of suggestions from the first referee report. Feedback welcome
summary: As single-aged populations containing stars spanning a range of masses but otherwise with similar properties, star clusters provide valuable testbeds for stellar evolution theory. The old, metal-rich, open cluster NGC 6791 is well studied, but the availability of asteroseismic observations of individual cluster members allows for a more in-depth analysis. Driven by mounting evidence that the solar assumption for convection used in almost all 1D stellar models is not adequate, and in light of the increased precision provided by modern data and asteroseismic constraints, we built and compared custom isochrones with varying values of the convective mixing length, $α_\text{MLT}$, to two clusters with well-determined ages: NGC 6791 and the well-studied, metal-poor globular cluster M92. For both clusters, we found that the best-fitting mixing length parameter decreases monotonically as a function of evolutionary phase, finding values between $0.98-1.10α_{\odot}$ for NGC 6791 and $1.16-1.21α_{\odot}$ for M92. In NGC 6791, this corresponds to an 18% decrease in the best fitting mixing length between the main sequence turn-off and upper end of the red giant branch. The degree of variation found within this one object is therefore comparable to variation across the literature in $α_\text{MLT}$ fits for other non-solar targets, calling single-valued $α_\text{MLT}$ fits to clusters into question. It is also consistent with $\log g$-$α_\text{MLT}$ trends predicted by higher-fidelity, 3D convection analyses. Our results therefore illustrate the need for more flexibility in our treatment of the mixing length in isochrones to properly model clusters.

AI.tldr: Custom isochrones with a free mixing length parameter α_MLT fit to NGC 6791 and M92 reveal that the best-fitting α_MLT decreases monotonically with evolutionary phase, questioning single-valued α_MLT calibrations for clusters.
AI.motivation: Nearly all 1D stellar models adopt the solar-calibrated mixing length, which mounting evidence shows is inadequate; asteroseismology of individual cluster members now offers the precision needed to test this assumption directly.
AI.method: Built and compared custom isochrones with varying α_MLT against two clusters with well-determined ages—the old, metal-rich open cluster NGC 6791 and the metal-poor globular cluster M92—using asteroseismic constraints on individual members.
AI.result: Best-fitting α_MLT decreases monotonically with evolutionary phase: 0.98–1.10 α_sun for NGC 6791 and 1.16–1.21 α_sun for M92. In NGC 6791 this is an 18% decrease between the main-sequence turn-off and the upper red giant branch, comparable to the spread across literature fits for non-solar targets.
AI.conclusion: The intra-cluster variation in α_MLT rivals inter-study scatter, undermining single-valued α_MLT fits for clusters and aligning with log g–α_MLT trends from 3D convection analyses; isochrones need a more flexible treatment of mixing length.

title: 3D Binary Evolution of a Merging Binary Black Hole Progenitor
summary: Mass transfer is a highly dynamical 3D process that spans evolutionary timescales in binary stars. It is key to the production of gravitational waves through formation of binary black holes and other double compact objects. We integrate global 3D hydrodynamics into stellar evolutionary modeling to resolve mass transfer across nuclear timescales. We employ the shellular approximation in the stellar evolution code MESA to map a 3D spatial structure by equipotential shells in the Roche geometry to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally-distorted surfaces. We employ the method of time-incremented multiscale evolution to alternate between stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span large timescales with dynamical feedback. We employ this framework to examine a likely merging binary black hole progenitor system of a low-metallicity 30Msol donor star and 9.3Msol black hole from the end of the main sequence to core Carbon depletion. We modeled two complete mass transfer phases in 3D while self-consistently accounting for stellar evolution. These comprised a thermal-timescale early Case B phase and a nuclear-timescale late Case B phase. The prescription of Kolb & Ritter (1990) closely predicted the results of 3D evolution, except at the end of the first phase of mass transfer; our 3D model remained well-contained by the outer Lagrange point, despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow during this stage. We find incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly impact expected merger times. Our model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions. L2/L3 outflows formed even while underflowing those equipotentials. Our model suggests these outflows can be neglected for the evolution of similar systems, but were dense enough to potentially impact X-ray observations.

AI.tldr: The authors couple global 3D hydrodynamics with MESA stellar evolution via a shellular-equipotential mapping and time-incremented multiscale alternation, and apply it to a low-metallicity 30 M☉ donor transferring mass onto a 9.3 M☉ BH through two Case B phases. 3D evolution agrees closely with Kolb & Ritter (1990) except at the end of the thermal-timescale phase, where the 3D model stays bound within L3 contrary to 1D L3-overflow predictions; merger times are largely unaffected.
AI.motivation: Mass transfer in binaries is fundamentally a 3D, highly dynamical process spanning evolutionary timescales and is central to forming binary black holes and other double compact objects. Standard 1D stellar evolution cannot self-consistently resolve the three-dimensional, tidally distorted mass-transfer geometry, so the accuracy of common prescriptions (e.g., L2/L3 overflow criteria) remains uncertain for gravitational-wave progenitor systems.
AI.method: Global 3D hydrodynamics is integrated into stellar evolutionary modeling. The shellular approximation in MESA maps 3D spatial structure onto equipotential shells in Roche geometry to preserve hydrostatic equilibrium across tidally distorted surfaces. A time-incremented multiscale evolution scheme alternates stellar evolution and 3D hydrodynamics to span long timescales with dynamical feedback. The framework is applied to a likely merging BBH progenitor: a low-metallicity 30 M☉ donor with a 9.3 M☉ BH, evolved from the end of the main sequence to core carbon depletion, covering an early thermal-timescale Case B phase and a late nuclear-timescale Case B phase.
AI.result: Two complete mass-transfer phases were modeled in 3D with self-consistent stellar evolution. The Kolb & Ritter (1990) prescription closely predicted the 3D results, except at the end of the first (thermal-timescale) phase, where the 3D model remained well contained within the outer Lagrange point despite 1D predictions of substantial L3 overflow. L2/L3 outflows formed even while the model underflowed those equipotentials. Incorporating 3D hydrodynamics during Case B mass transfer did not significantly alter expected merger times.
AI.conclusion: The model never overflowed L3 as predicted by 1D prescriptions, and L2/L3 outflows arose even below those equipotentials. Such outflows appear negligible for the evolutionary outcome of similar systems but were dense enough to potentially affect X-ray observations. The framework demonstrates that coupled multiscale 3D hydrodynamics plus stellar evolution is a viable route to validating 1D mass-transfer prescriptions for GW progenitors.

title: TWIN-2: Timing Solar Radio Bursts between 180-350 MHz Against GOES and Aditya-L1 X-ray Detections
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Includes a 2-page appendix listing the analysed events
summary: We have conducted continuous solar observations for approximately two and half years using the Two-Element Interferometer (TWIN) at Gauribidanur Radio Observatory (RRI). During which several solar events have been detected. Our observational period coincides with the maximum events phase of the Solar Cycle 25, providing us opportunity to analyse the evolution of the solar activity. Our analysis of two and half years data show a clear increase in the occurrences of solar events, which is consistent with the expected rise in the solar activity towards the peak phase of the Solar Cycle 25. We further investigate the detected solar radio events using X-ray observations from the space based Aditya-L1 and the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) satellites. For the automated detection of SRBs, a machine learning suite has been trained. This also serves as an instrument for space weather monitoring. On the 7th of November 2025, a solar storm was detected by our pipeline in realtime. A brief overview of the data-processing pipeline, along with the RFI mitigation techniques employed to identify and characterize the solar events, is also presented. Observation data of two and a half years of TWIN is available for public access. The data has been used in student training programmes on solar radio data analysis, with students carrying out the analysis and contributing to the initial analysis of the detected events.

AI.tldr: Two-and-a-half years of continuous solar observations with the TWIN interferometer at Gauribidanur reveal a clear rise in solar radio event occurrence consistent with Solar Cycle 25's approach to maximum, with events cross-checked against X-ray data from Aditya-L1 and GOES, and an ML-based automated solar radio burst detection pipeline demonstrated in real time.
AI.motivation: Solar Cycle 25 is approaching its maximum, offering a window to track the evolution of solar activity. The authors aim to characterize solar radio event rates over this period and to enable automated, real-time space-weather monitoring, while also making TWIN data publicly available for education.
AI.method: Continuous solar monitoring for ~2.5 years with the Two-Element Interferometer (TWIN) at Gauribidanur Radio Observatory; statistical analysis of event occurrence over time; cross-comparison of detected solar radio events with X-ray observations from Aditya-L1 and GOES; a trained machine-learning suite for automated solar radio burst (SRB) detection; a data-processing pipeline incorporating radio-frequency interference (RFI) mitigation techniques.
AI.result: A clear increase in the occurrence of solar events over the 2.5-year dataset, consistent with the expected rise toward Solar Cycle 25 maximum. A real-time solar storm detection by the pipeline on 7 November 2025. TWIN data are publicly available and have been used in student training programs, with students contributing to initial event analysis.
AI.conclusion: TWIN's sustained monitoring, combined with multi-instrument X-ray validation, RFI-mitigated processing, and ML-based automated detection, provides a working space-weather monitoring capability and an open dataset supporting both solar activity studies and education.

title: Hard X-ray flux rope anchor points in the October 2024 X9 flare
summary: In recent studies, signatures of non-thermal hard X-ray (HXR) emission at the anchor point of erupting flux ropes were reported, suggesting that accelerated electrons trapped in the erupting flux ropes can reach the chromosphere and produce Bremsstrahlung emission there. We investigated the HXR sources observed during the impulsive phase of the X9-class flare SOL2024-10-03T12:18 from AR 13842 and assessed whether any of the HXR sources are associated with the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. We analysed the evolution and location of the flare ribbon sources and coronal dimmings to diagnose the eruption process by using multi-vantage point data from the Solar Orbiter and Earth-orbiting instruments. We combined this with a pre-eruption non-linear force-free magnetic field extrapolation to reconstruct the initial magnetic connectivity and compare it to the observed flare ribbons and dimming locations. The magnetic field extrapolation shows two flux ropes before the flare onset. Tether-cutting reconnection during the impulsive phase of the flare results in a larger erupting flux rope formed by the reconnection of the two pre-existing flux ropes. The Spectrometer/Telescope for Imaging X-rays on Solar Orbiter observes at least four distinct HXR sources: two flare footpoints and two additional outer sources at the anchor points of the erupting flux rope. These observations corroborate earlier speculations that non-thermal electrons trapped in the erupting flux rope precipitate along the field lines into the denser chromosphere.

AI.tldr: Analysis of the X9-class flare SOL2024-10-03T12:18 from AR 13842 shows hard X-ray sources at the anchor points of the erupting flux rope, supporting electron trapping in the rope and precipitation into the chromosphere.
AI.motivation: Recent reports of non-thermal hard X-ray (HXR) signatures at the anchor points of erupting flux ropes suggest that accelerated electrons trapped in the rope reach the chromosphere and emit Bremsstrahlung. This study tests and diagnoses that scenario for a well-observed X9 flare.
AI.method: Multi-vantage-point observations (Solar Orbiter and Earth-orbiting instruments) were used to track flare ribbon sources and coronal dimmings to diagnose the eruption. These were combined with a pre-eruption non-linear force-free (NLFFF) field extrapolation to reconstruct initial magnetic connectivity, compared against observed ribbon and dimming locations; STIX on Solar Orbiter imaged the HXR sources.
AI.result: The NLFFF extrapolation reveals two flux ropes before flare onset; tether-cutting reconnection during the impulsive phase merges them into a larger erupting flux rope. STIX detects at least four distinct HXR sources: two flare footpoints and two additional outer sources located at the anchor points of the erupting flux rope.
AI.conclusion: HXR emission at the flux-rope anchor points corroborates earlier speculation that non-thermal electrons trapped in the erupting flux rope precipitate along field lines into the denser chromosphere.

title: Mauve Observations of the Eclipsing Binary System $β$ Lyrae
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to Nature Astronomy
summary: We present a broadband, synoptic observing campaign of the complex eclipsing binary system $β$ Lyr, obtained with the first commercial astronomical satellite, Mauve, developed and operated by Blue Skies Space Ltd. Mauve's capabilities have resulted in the first multiphase monitoring of $β$ Lyr, covering UV and optical photometry, as well as low-resolution spectrophotometry, including the phase-folded mapping of the intensity of a number of emission lines. The different components in its spectrum vary in very different ways, indicative of a system with a number of physical components. Our data show that while most of the components show repeatable cycle-to-cycle variability, the thus far hardly observed UV emission (2000-3000 Angstrom) varies significantly from one cycle to the other, pointing to the need for simultaneous observations to understand and model the system. These observations reveal that the ultraviolet-emitting structures in this benchmark interacting binary evolve on timescales of individual orbits, challenging the assumption of a stationary accretion geometry commonly adopted in models of interacting binary stars. The quality of the data set and the fresh view that they bring to a well studied, but still poorly understood object demonstrate the scientific value of small telescopes with focused scientific capabilities, as well as the value of a new generation of commercial astronomical instrumentation.

AI.tldr: A broadband synoptic campaign with the commercial Mauve satellite provides the first multiphase UV and optical monitoring of β Lyr, revealing UV-emitting structures that evolve on single-orbit timescales and challenging stationary accretion-geometry assumptions.
AI.motivation: β Lyr is a benchmark interacting eclipsing binary that remains poorly understood despite extensive study; its multiple spectral components vary differently, and prior UV coverage was sparse, so simultaneous, phase-resolved multiwavelength monitoring is needed to disentangle its physical components and test whether the accretion geometry is stationary.
AI.method: A broadband, synoptic observing campaign using the first commercial astronomical satellite, Mauve (Blue Skies Space Ltd), yielding the first multiphase monitoring of β Lyr: UV and optical photometry plus low-resolution spectrophotometry, including phase-folded mapping of emission-line intensities.
AI.result: Spectral components vary in markedly different ways, indicating multiple physical components. Most components show repeatable cycle-to-cycle variability, but the previously scarcely observed UV emission (2000–3000 Å) varies significantly between cycles, motivating simultaneous observations for modeling. The UV-emitting structures evolve on timescales of individual orbits.
AI.conclusion: The assumption of a stationary accretion geometry commonly used in interacting binary models is challenged. The data quality demonstrates the scientific value of small, focused-capability telescopes and of a new generation of commercial astronomical instrumentation.

title: Spatio-Temporal Evolution of a Steady Transition Region Downflow above a Sunspot
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures and 1 Table, accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: Super-Sonic Downflows (SSDs) are usually observed above sunspots as redshifted peaks in lower Transition Region (TR) spectral lines and can last from a few minutes to several hours. Utilising high-cadence, $\sim$3 hour long repeated-raster mode observations from Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), we investigate the spatio-temporal dynamics of such a downflow event above NOAA active region 12135. Triple Gaussian fitting to TR spectral lines, along with Non-Force Free Field (NFFF) extrapolation and Differential Emission Measure (DEM) analysis, is performed to study this event. Downflow is initially observed in both the umbral and penumbral regions. Over time, the penumbral downflow fades, while the umbral downflow strengthens and appears as a single structure initially but eventually splits into two spatial segments. The calculated average properties, including downflow speed, electron density, and mass flux for this event, align with established studies. Simultaneous evolution in overlying coronal loops is also observed using imaging data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA). DEM analysis of the coronal emission over the downflow region indicates corresponding changes in cool ($\log_{10}[T/\mathrm{K}] \in [5.5, 5.6]$) coronal plasma. As suggested by recurrent transient brightenings observed in the nearby region in coronal channels and the corresponding fan-spine magnetic topology identified from NFFF extrapolations, magnetic reconnection occurring in this region is proposed to be the cause of this evolution. Our analysis revealed that changes in the morphology of TR downflows are closely associated with evolution of overlying coronal loops.

AI.tldr: A ~3-hour IRIS repeated-raster study of a super-sonic downflow (SSD) above NOAA AR 12135 reveals that its morphology splits and evolves in close association with the overlying coronal loops, with magnetic reconnection in a fan-spine topology proposed as the driver.
AI.motivation: Super-sonic downflows above sunspots, seen as redshifted peaks in lower Transition Region lines, last from minutes to hours, yet their spatio-temporal dynamics and coupling to the overlying corona remain poorly characterized.
AI.method: High-cadence (~3 h) repeated-raster IRIS observations of AR 12135; triple-Gaussian fitting of TR spectral lines to derive downflow speed, electron density, and mass flux; Non-Force-Free Field (NFFF) extrapolation for magnetic topology; DEM analysis of AIA coronal emission; comparison with coronal loop evolution.
AI.result: Downflow appears initially in both umbra and penumbra; the penumbral component fades while the umbral one strengthens, first as a single structure then splitting into two spatial segments. Average speed, density, and mass flux agree with prior studies. DEM shows corresponding changes in cool coronal plasma (log10[T/K] in [5.5, 5.6]); recurrent transient coronal brightenings and a fan-spine topology support reconnection as the driver.
AI.conclusion: Morphological evolution of TR SSDs is closely tied to the evolution of overlying coronal loops, with magnetic reconnection in a fan-spine configuration proposed as the underlying mechanism.

title: Superoutburst Precursors in the Faint SU UMa-type Dwarf Nova KSP-OT-201602a
comment: 14 pages, J. Korean Astron. Soc. (JKAS) accepted
summary: We present the discovery and photometric study of an SU UMa-type dwarf nova (DN) KSP-OT-201602a. Korea Microlensing Telescope Network Supernova Program data covered almost four years from 2016 to 2019 in BVI-bands for this field, and discovered this faint SU UMa-type DN. Two superoutbursts (SOs: S1 and S2) and two normal outbursts (NOs: N1 and N2) are observed of which peak brightnesses are V = 18.95 mag (S1), V = 18.69 mag (S2) and V = 19.37 mag (N1), V = 19.11 mag (N2). The phase dispersion minimization analysis on superhump of S1 gives the superhump period of 1.52 hr (= 91.2 minutes = 0.06333 days). The magnitude amplitudes for the SOs are 4.34 mag (S1) and 4.60 mag (S2), and those for the NOs are 3.98 mag (N1) and 4.18 mag (N2). The durations of the SOs are 11.39 days (S1) and 12.00 days (S2), and those for the NOs are 2.68 days (N1) and 3.38 days (N2). Clear evidence of a precursor is identified in S1 before the SO peak and this supports the hypothesis that precursor is an NO triggerring an SO and the superhump, while a potential precursor based on limited data is only observed in S2. While the amplitudes of the SOs appear typical for SU UMa-type DNe, their durations seem to be quite short which might require further model calculations in the future.

AI.tldr: Discovery and photometric study of the SU UMa-type dwarf nova KSP-OT-201602a, which shows two short-duration superoutbursts and two normal outbursts over four years of KMTNet data.
AI.motivation: To characterize a newly discovered faint SU UMa-type dwarf nova identified in the KMTNet Supernova Program field, and to study its outburst properties and superhump period.
AI.method: Four years (2016-2019) of BVI-band photometric monitoring by the Korea Microlensing Telescope Network Supernova Program; phase dispersion minimization (PDM) analysis of the superhump.
AI.result: Two superoutbursts (peaks V=18.95, 18.69 mag; amplitudes 4.34, 4.60 mag; durations 11.39, 12.00 d) and two normal outbursts (peaks V=19.37, 19.11 mag; amplitudes 3.98, 4.18 mag; durations 2.68, 3.38 d). Superhump period = 1.52 hr (91.2 min). Clear precursor evidence in S1, potential precursor in S2.
AI.conclusion: Amplitudes are typical of SU UMa-type DNe, but outburst durations appear unusually short, warranting further model calculations. The precursor in S1 supports the hypothesis that a precursor is a normal outburst triggering a superoutburst and superhump.

title: Connecting Coronal Loop Scaling Laws and Kink Wave Heating: An Analytical and Numerical Study
summary: Turbulent dissipation of kink waves has been proposed as one of the mechanisms responsible for the observed high coronal temperatures. We test this hypothesis by examining the effect of this heating mechanism on coronal loops. The coronal loop static and dynamic behaviour is investigated under the assumption that the heating in the loop is primarily provided by kink wave dissipation. The heating term is borrowed from the recently developed UAWSoM model. Loop modelling is done in 1D using three different methods: one analytical following the principles first set in the RTV scaling laws, and two numerical: one based on the setup used to derive the RTVS scaling laws, and UAWSoM. We provide scaling laws and estimate density, temperature, and pressure, as well as kink wave heating rate and kink wave energy density needed to counteract energy loss by thermal conduction and radiative cooling. Estimates of kink wave energy density needed to heat the loop to 1 MK correspond to maximum velocity amplitudes of around 35 km s$^{-1}$ near the loop apex. Loop radius, density contrast and filling factor are found to affect the predictions significantly. The two numerical methods agree to a high degree. The analytical method predicts that $W_\textrm{k} \propto PL^{-2/3}$, while the two numerical methods show a wider range of scaling exponents which depend on the location in the loop. UAWSoM simulations suggest that loops may exhibit dynamic behaviour for a wide range of loop conditions, which may include thermal non-equilibrium cycles and periods of emerging and dissipating slow waves. Overall, estimates of kink wave energy density and scaling laws provide observational constraints on the importance of the proposed kink wave heating mechanism, with the current preliminary results suggesting that the uniturbulent kink wave heating may be a significant source of energy and heat in coronal loops.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether turbulent dissipation of kink waves can heat coronal loops, using one analytical RTV-style model and two numerical approaches (RTVS setup and UAWSoM). Estimates of required kink wave energy density correspond to velocity amplitudes of ~35 km/s at the loop apex, with loop radius, density contrast, and filling factor strongly affecting predictions; the authors conclude uniturbulent kink wave heating may be a significant coronal loop heating source.
AI.motivation: Turbulent dissipation of kink waves has been proposed as a mechanism explaining observed high coronal temperatures, but its effect on coronal loop heating had not been systematically tested against loop static and dynamic behavior.
AI.method: The heating term is taken from the UAWSoM model and loop modelling is performed in 1D via three methods: an analytical approach based on RTV scaling law principles; a numerical setup used to derive the RTVS scaling laws; and UAWSoM. The authors derive scaling laws and estimate density, temperature, pressure, kink wave heating rate, and kink wave energy density required to balance thermal conduction and radiative cooling losses.
AI.result: Heating a loop to 1 MK requires kink wave energy densities corresponding to maximum velocity amplitudes of ~35 km/s near the apex. Loop radius, density contrast, and filling factor significantly affect predictions. The two numerical methods agree closely, while the analytical method yields W_k ∝ P L^{-2/3} and the numerical methods show a wider range of scaling exponents depending on position along the loop. UAWSoM simulations indicate loops may be dynamic across a wide range of conditions, including thermal non-equilibrium cycles and episodes of emerging and dissipating slow waves.
AI.conclusion: The derived energy density estimates and scaling laws provide observational constraints on kink wave heating. Preliminary results suggest uniturbulent kink wave heating may be a significant source of energy and heat in coronal loops.

title: Multiple blobs following a coronal mass ejection
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in RAA
summary: In this paper, we study a partial filament eruption, which generated a C4.1 class two-ribbon flare and a wide coronal mass ejection (CME) propagating in the northeast direction on 2023 March 20. The long, sigmoidal filament in active region 13258 is composed of two parts: the eruptive part and remaining part. Both of them are supported by magnetic flux ropes. The separation of two ribbons persist for ~12 hr, with the separation speeds decreasing from 0.26-5.62 to 0.13-0.53 km/s observed in H$α$ and 304 Å. A thin, curved current sheet follows the CME and extends in the northeast direction. Eight and seven bright blobs are found to move outward along the current sheet observed by SOHO/LASCO and STEREO-A/COR2, respectively. In LASCO images, the apparent speeds, lifetime, maximal height, and width of the blobs are 378-871 km/s, 7-84 minutes, 2.94-6.25\,$R_{\sun}$, and 38.8-225.4 Mm. In COR2 images, the apparent speeds, lifetime, maximal height, and width of the blobs are 336-712 km/s, 20-100 minutes, 4.09-7.61\,$R_{\sun}$, and 102.9-318.3 Mm. A positive correlation is found between the lifetime and maximal height, suggesting that blobs with longer lifetime propagate further from the solar surface. The total duration of blobs is >8 hr, which is consistent with ongoing flare reconnection manifested by persistent ribbon separation in the chromosphere. The aspect ratio (28-37) of the current sheet is probably larger than the critical value, suggesting that the blobs following the CME are possibly generated by tearing-mode instability of the current sheet.

AI.tldr: A C4.1 two-ribbon flare and NE-directed CME on 2023 March 20 arise from a partial eruption of a sigmoidal filament in AR 13258; blobs moving outward along a thin curved current sheet are likely generated by tearing-mode instability, sustained over >8 hr consistent with ongoing reconnection.
AI.motivation: To characterize a partial filament eruption and its associated flare–CME–current-sheet system, and to test whether propagating blobs along the post-CME current sheet originate from tearing-mode instability, linking them to prolonged magnetic reconnection.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength and multi-viewpoint analysis: Hα and 304 Å imaging for flare ribbons (separation speeds, duration); SOHO/LASCO and STEREO-A/COR2 coronagraphs for the CME, current sheet, and blobs (apparent speeds, lifetime, maximal height, width); magnetic flux-rope interpretation of the two filament parts; aspect-ratio assessment of the current sheet against a critical value for tearing instability.
AI.result: Ribbon separation persists ~12 hr with speeds decreasing from 0.26–5.62 to 0.13–0.53 km/s. A thin curved current sheet extends NE behind the CME. Eight (LASCO) and seven (COR2) blobs move outward: LASCO speeds 378–871 km/s, lifetimes 7–84 min, heights 2.94–6.25 R_sun, widths 38.8–225.4 Mm; COR2 speeds 336–712 km/s, lifetimes 20–100 min, heights 4.09–7.61 R_sun, widths 102.9–318.3 Mm. Lifetime correlates positively with maximal height; total blob duration >8 hr, consistent with persistent ribbon separation; current-sheet aspect ratio 28–37 probably exceeds the critical value.
AI.conclusion: The partial eruption involves two flux-rope-supported filament segments, with the CME trailing a curved current sheet hosting outward-propagating blobs. The long-lived (>8 hr) blob activity and ribbon separation indicate sustained flare reconnection, and the supercritical current-sheet aspect ratio suggests blobs are generated by tearing-mode instability.

title: Tracing Magnetic Helicity in Interplanetary Space. A Multi-Spacecraft Analysis of the 2024 March 23 ICME
summary: We study the evolution of the magnetic helicity content of an ICME event by inferring its magnetic-field-related quantities at different stages between the Sun and Earth using remote sensing and in-situ observations. We study an eruptive X1.1 flare/CME event and its associated ICME originating from NOAA active region (AR) 13614 on 2024 March 23 00:58 UT. Using magnetogram data of the AR during the flaring event, along with non-linear force-free (NLFF) magnetic field modeling, we reconstruct the magnetic field in the solar corona and analyze its magnetic helicity budget. The helicity is also tracked in-situ in the heliosphere using four well radially-aligned spacecraft (Solar Orbiter at 0.39 AU, BepiColombo at 0.58 AU, STEREO-A at 0.96 AU and Wind at 0.99 AU) measuring the ICME magnetic field signature. We use different force-free magnetic field models (Lundquist, Gold-Hoyle) to evaluate the helicity values at each spacecraft. With the Gold-Hoyle-based model (expansion-modified force-free model, 3DCORE), we also reconstruct the ICME and its propagation in the heliosphere. We ultimately compare the results obtained for each model and spacecraft to the values computed in the corona to give a general understanding of how the event's magnetic field evolved. The NLFF modeling of the AR indicates a left-handed (negative helicity) flux rope (FR) positioned along a slightly northeast-southwest axis, in agreement with chromospheric and coronal observations (H-alpha, SDO/AIA), and yields a helicity budget computed of $-2.16\pm1.32\times10^{41}~\text{Mx}^2$. The helicity inferred from in-situ modeling methods reveals values in a similar range ($-2.0\pm1.0\times10^{41}~\text{Mx}^2$), but is highly sensitive to the spacecraft crossing position through the ICME. It appears that the results given by 3DCORE are more consistent between all spacecraft, as well as with the values inferred at the AR.

AI.tldr: The paper tracks the magnetic helicity of a 2024 March 23 X1.1 flare/CME (AR 13614) from the corona to 1 AU using NLFF modeling and multi-spacecraft in-situ force-free fits, finding a consistent left-handed (negative) helicity budget of roughly −2×10^41 Mx².
AI.motivation: Understanding how the magnetic helicity of an interplanetary coronal mass ejection (ICME) is conserved or evolves from the solar source to Earth requires linking coronal helicity budgets to in-situ measurements; this event offers a rare opportunity with four radially aligned spacecraft.
AI.method: NLFF magnetic field modeling of AR 13614 magnetograms during the flare yields the coronal flux-rope helicity budget. In-situ helicity is inferred from force-free fits (Lundquist and Gold-Hoyle) to ICME magnetic signatures at Solar Orbiter (0.39 AU), BepiColombo (0.58 AU), STEREO-A (0.96 AU) and Wind (0.99 AU); the Gold-Hoyle-based expansion-modified model (3DCORE) also reconstructs ICME propagation.
AI.result: NLFF modeling indicates a left-handed (negative helicity) flux rope along a slightly NE–SW axis, consistent with H-alpha and SDO/AIA observations, giving a helicity budget of −2.16±1.32×10^41 Mx². In-situ methods give comparable values (−2.0±1.0×10^41 Mx²) but are highly sensitive to the spacecraft crossing position through the ICME; 3DCORE results are more consistent across spacecraft and with the AR value.
AI.conclusion: The ICME's negative helicity is approximately conserved from corona to 1 AU, and the expansion-modified Gold-Hoyle (3DCORE) model provides the most robust, cross-spacecraft-consistent helicity estimates.
